vignette: The typhoon hit during his sophomore year of college, tearing the roof off the lower level of his apartment building. Duy remembered the sudden shift in atmospheric pressure, the glass shattering inward, and the ceiling joists groaning. He threw himself against a load-bearing pillar, neck cricked at a sharp angle, pressing his cervical spine against the rough wood as water and splintered timber rained down. For forty-three minutes, he held that position, muscles corded tight, waiting for the structure to give. When the winds finally died, he emerged with a lasting ache in his neck that never quite faded, a physical echo of that desperate brace. In the months that followed, Duy navigated his days through a new set of bodily warnings. The neck pain became a specific trigger. During a late-night wireframe review last spring, the familiar tightness crept up his spine as he leaned toward his ergonomic monitor. He froze, his breath catching, and pushed his chair back, leaving the office without a word. Around the same time, episodes of feeling physically unwell began. A vague nausea would coil in his stomach, unprovoked by food or fatigue, often arriving after major storms or the distant rumble of summer thunder. He learned to cancel plans and stay in bed, certain his body was simply rejecting the shifting atmosphere. Trauma-related events functioned as another trigger; walking past a hardware store that sold structural steel beams or hearing a contractor's jackhammer nearby would make him stop mid-stride, his shoulders hiking toward his ears, waiting for the collapse. The memories arrived in fragments that refused to settle into a coherent film. Sometimes, a sudden wave of terror struck without any image, leaving him staring blankly at a color palette on his screen, hands cold and knees weak until the emotional intensity receded. Other times, the past returned through taste. He would taste the metallic grit of wet drywall and old wood, so vividly that he would drop his stylus and wipe his mouth, half-expecting debris between his teeth. The narrative of that night felt stubbornly unbelievable. He found himself double-checking weather archives and structural engineering forums, a persistent thought that the story had to be a dream, that no ordinary building could ever actually come apart like that. The doubts and the physical tension existed side by side, neither explaining the other. As the weeks turned to months, his daily environment grew quieter. He stopped attending the company's Friday design critiques, noticing with detached observation that his colleagues' smiles felt rehearsed, that people were not what they seemed. He found himself sitting at his desk long after his team logged off, the office humming around him while he felt isolated and set apart from the easy banter. He believed he no longer belonged anywhere, canceling his summer trip with his sister because the idea of traveling felt like asking for a disaster to follow. The consequences accumulated quietly; he submitted prototypes with delayed hand-tracking and skipped morning stand-ups, his neck perpetually stiff from bracing against invisible loads. By the time he reached out to a clinic at twenty-two, the routine of his work had fractured. What finally brought him through the doors was a client presentation where the familiar wave of physical unwellness struck mid-pitch. He had to step into the hallway, hands gripping the doorframe, realizing he could no longer outrun the silence he had built. He was hoping someone could help him untangle the knot in his shoulders and find a way to rest his mind, terrified that if he did not seek relief, he would remain forever stranded between a past that felt like a dream and a present that no longer felt like his own.
